facts.text: The film's working titles were "Drag Race" and "The Ghost of the Dragstrip Hollow" before AIP settled on the release title.
This was a fast one: AFI records production running from May 11 to late May 1959, with a July release. Quick, cheap and aimed straight at drive-ins.
The flood-channel race crash: the deep pool of water vanishes by the time the motorcycle cop arrives. Not enough time passes for that much water to drain away.
It's a sequel to AIP's 1958 Hot Rod Gang, and the cast carries over, including Jody Fair (Lois Cavendish) and Henry McCann (Dave).
Writer-producer Lou Rusoff was AIP boss Sam Arkoff's brother-in-law and the studio's most prolific screenwriter. He also wrote The Day the World Ended and It Conquered the World.
Writer-producer Lou Rusoff died in 1963 of brain cancer while editing Beach Party. This film is often called a forerunner of that Beach Party series.
Drag racer "TV" Tommy Ivo plays himself, and both his white-top Model T and his Buick-powered dragster in the film were his real cars.
Tommy Ivo started as a child actor in I Remember Mama (1948). He was later ranked No. 25 on the NHRA's Top 50 Drivers list.
Tommy Ivo also played Herbie Bailey on The Donna Reed Show (1959-61). He raced a twin-Buick dragster billed as the first gas dragster under nine seconds.
AFI notes the film was shot at Amco Studios in Los Angeles. Rusoff kept costs down by limiting the number of sets and locations.
Co-star Russ Bender (journalist Tom Hendry) was a B-movie regular: he appeared in The Amazing Colossal Man, War of the Colossal Beast and It Conquered the World.
Jody Fair (Lois Cavendish) worked as a secretary in MGM's law department before acting. She turned down a Playboy centerfold offer and later went into real estate.
Continuity slip: the cook Frenchie dances in front of the counter, throws up his hands, walks off, then reappears doing the exact same thing.
Jimmie Maddin, credited as music coordinator, wrote "Tongue Tied" for the film. AIP released the songs on American International Records.
Songwriter Bruce Johnston co-wrote "I Promise You" for this film. He later joined the Beach Boys.
Reviewers said the sparse plot and many pop numbers made it "little more than publicity for the tunes" released on AIP's own record label.
The film's girl-group number is a dead-on parody of the girl groups popular at the time. Fans count it among the highlights.
Actress Nancy Anderson (Nita) made her screen debut in this film.
The film spoofs AIP's own 1950s monster and drag-racing movies. One critic said it's tired of the car-movie formula the studio kept churning out.
Critic Dennis Schwartz graded it a D: "A dreadful hot rod teen comedy for the drive-in crowd. This one stinks even for AIP." He did enjoy the hipster slang.
Paul Blaisdell, AIP's top monster-maker, recycled the She-Creature suit from The She-Creature (1956) and the alien head from Invasion of the Saucer Men (1957) here.
Street Muscle's review says the film has "very little racing action, even less hot rods," but plenty of hokey slang.
In January 1960 the film was widely shown at drive-ins on a double bill with The Diary of a High School Bride (1959).
The first mention of a ghost, in a film called Ghost of Dragstrip Hollow, comes about 40 minutes in. The movie runs only about 64 minutes.
Blaisdell's Beast with a Million Eyes (1955) prop was left in direct sunlight until it fell apart.
The closing credit reads "The Endest, Man," a joke on the usual "The End."
Watch the saxophonist's close-up: his fingers never move on the keys, so he isn't even pretending to play.
Blaisdell has said the She-Creature costume "just wasn't the same costume any more" after AIP had him alter it for reuse.
Blaisdell's tearful unmasking speech name-drops his earlier AIP work. It was his last film, and no Hollywood paper ran his obituary when he died in 1983.
Blaisdell's monster-suit complaint that AIP didn't use him in Horrors of the Black Museum came true: he never worked on another film after this one.
